title: Anaerobic Fate of Pyruvate: Fermentation Pathways

quickSummary: In the absence of oxygen, fermentation pathways regenerate the cytosolic NAD⁺ required by GAPDH in glycolysis. In lactic acid fermentation, Lactate Dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate directly to lactic acid (3C) without CO₂ release. In alcoholic fermentation (yeast), Pyruvate Decarboxylase (requiring TPP) decarboxylates pyruvate to acetaldehyde (releasing CO₂), followed by reduction to ethanol (2C) by Alcohol Dehydrogenase (requiring Zn²⁺). Fermentation captures <7% of glucose free energy, and yeast undergoes autolysis at ~13% ethanol.

summaryBox.takeaway: Fermentation regenerates cytosolic NAD⁺. Lactic acid produces 3C lactate without CO₂; Alcoholic fermentation produces 2C ethanol + CO₂. Fermentation extracts <7% total glucose energy.

conceptBreakdown.content:
In the absence of molecular oxygen ($\text{O}_2$), cells cannot regenerate mitochondrial $\text{NAD}^+$ via electron transport. Fermentation pathways re-oxidize cytosolic $\text{NADH}$ back to $\text{NAD}^+$, allowing the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) step of glycolysis to continue producing $2\text{ ATP}$ net per glucose.

- **Lactic Acid Fermentation**:
  - Occurs in lactic acid bacteria (*Lactobacillus*) and vertebrate skeletal muscle under vigorous hypoxic exercise.
  - Catalyzed by **Lactate Dehydrogenase** ($\text{LDH}$):
    $$\mathbf{\text{Pyruvate} + \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+ \xrightarrow{\text{Lactate Dehydrogenase}} \text{Lactic Acid (3C)} + \text{NAD}^+}$$
  - No carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) is released (both pyruvate and lactate are 3-carbon compounds).

- **Alcoholic Fermentation**:
  - Occurs in brewing/baking yeast (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*) and certain microorganisms.
  - Operates via a two-step sequence:
    1. **Decarboxylation**: **Pyruvate Decarboxylase** (requires Thiamine Pyrophosphate, $\text{TPP}$, and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$) converts Pyruvate ($3\text{C}$) into Acetaldehyde ($2\text{C}$) with the release of $\text{CO}_2\uparrow$.
    2. **Reduction**: **Alcohol Dehydrogenase** (requires $\text{Zn}^{2+}$) reduces Acetaldehyde to Ethanol ($2\text{C}$), re-oxidizing $\text{NADH}$ to $\text{NAD}^+$.

conceptBreakdown.title: 3.1 Fermentation Bioenergetics & Yeast Toxicity Limits
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
FERMENTATION BIOENERGETICS
                        
   1. Lactic Acid: Pyruvate + NADH + H⁺ ──[Lactate Dehydrogenase]──► Lactic Acid + NAD⁺
   
   2. Alcoholic:   Pyruvate ──[Pyruvate Decarboxylase + TPP]──► Acetaldehyde + CO₂ ↑
                   Acetaldehyde + NADH + H⁺ ──[Alcohol Dehydrogenase + Zn²⁺]──► Ethanol + NAD⁺
conceptBreakdown.content:
- **Low Energetic Efficiency**: Less than $7\%$ of the total potential chemical energy present in a glucose molecule is trapped as ATP during fermentation. The remaining energy resides unreleased within the reduced end-products (ethanol or lactic acid) or is lost as heat.
- **Zero ETS Phosphorylation**: Fermentation produces ATP strictly by substrate-level phosphorylation during glycolysis ($2\text{ ATP}$ net per glucose); no proton gradients or oxidative phosphorylation occur.
- **Alcohol Toxicity Threshold**: Accumulation of ethanol above $\approx 13\%$ by volume is naturally toxic to yeast cells, disrupting membrane fluidity and leading to autolysis (self-poisoning).
